overview: The Samanids, a Persian dynasty ruling from Bukhara from 819 to 999, presided over the revival of Persian as a written language after two centuries of Arabic. Their court fed the poets and scholars of the Islamic Golden Age in Central Asia.

items.text: Avicenna was born near Bukhara; his Canon of Medicine remained a standard medical text in Europe and the Islamic world into the seventeenth century.
Al-Biruni was born in Khwarazm and began his work in astronomy and mathematics as the Samanid age ended.
Rudaki, called the father of Persian poetry, wrote at the court of Nasr II.
Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh, the Persian epic, under Samanid rule; he finished it in 1010.
Bowls and plates from Nishapur and Samarkand carry black Kufic proverbs on white slip.
Persian became a language of court and literature beside Arabic; the vizier Bal'ami's Persian version of Tabari's history was made for the amir.
The dynasty was Sunni and patronized Hanafi scholars, and Bukhara became a center of Islamic learning.
Bukhara and Samarkand were the Silk Road's markets between China and the Islamic west.
Samanid silver dirhams were carried north along the Volga in such numbers that hoards of them turn up across Russia and Scandinavia.
The Persian literary revival shaped the Ghaznavid, Seljuk and later courts.
The mausoleum of the Samanids in Bukhara, a cube of patterned brick, is among the oldest surviving Islamic monuments in Central Asia.

fall.text: The Karakhanids took Bukhara in 999 while the Ghaznavids, once Samanid slave-governors, took Khurasan south of the Oxus.
